(1) Locator p. 61 = PDF p. 75, sec. 2.3.1.5 'Tone patterns': text reads exactly 'Lexical tone is demonstrated by pairs of words that differ only in their tonal value. Lexical tone in Kambari carries a very small semantic load. The following tone data indicates Kambari utilizes two level lexical tones. All the examples are in Auna Kambari, but the patterns are the same in the other two languages unless otherwise noted.' followed by noun patterns LL/HL/LH (no HH), LLL/LHL/LHH/HLL/HHH, imperative verbs 'nearly always LH' (exception zama LL), Salka bars word-initial H, fn. 21 tone elicited in isolation…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tsikimba (Auna Kambari) is described as a two-level-tone language with light lexical tone load (nouns LL/HL/LH, LLL/LHL/LHH/HLL/HHH; imperative verbs nearly always LH). The source gives no rule for the position of word stress; its only stress-related remark is that the root-final vowel becomes a reduced ('unstressed') /u/ ~ [ɨ]-like vowel when a suffix follows.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. For tone: Salka Kambari (not Tsikimba) disallows word-initial H; imperative verbs LH with a few LL exceptions (zama 'search').
new_statements.domain_note: Tone data elicited on isolated words (fn. 21, p. 61). The 'Unstressed /u/' remark concerns suffixed verb forms (root + iterative -sV etc.), i.e. word-internal vowel reduction, not phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Stark 2010 states (p. 40; App. B p. 196) that her 'Auna Kambari' description 'is based on the Tsikimba dialect as is spoken in Auna town' = tsik1238 / ISO kdl (other Auna Kambari dialects named: Tsishen, Tsugaunshi/Tsugaunshe). The same book also treats Agwara Kambari (Cishingini, asg) and Salka Kambari (Tsishingini, tsw, tsis1238) as co-languages; tone patterns are said to be shared except that Salka bars word-initial H. Glottolog's descriptive refs filed under tsik1238 (Hoffmann 1963, 1972 'Central Kambari') actually concern the Salka/Raba variety (tsis1238), so Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description for Tsikimba is effectively Stark 2010.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3.1 phonology (pp. 42-64): syllable/word patterns (2.3.1.4, pp. 59-61) and tone (2.3.1.5, pp. 61-63: two level lexical tones, very small semantic load, noun patterns LL/HL/LH, LLL/LHL/LHH/HLL/HHH, imperative verbs nearly always LH). No statement of where word stress falls anywhere in the book (only two hits for 'stress': one irrelevant, one the Appendix-B heading 'Unstressed /u/', p. 200, describing reduction of the root-final vowel before a suffix in Auna Kambari). Appendix B 'Tone' p. 203: under 20 minimal tone pairs; tone not.
